common_name: N'Joy Pothos (Compact Crisp White-Green Variegated Pothos)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained potting mix in bright indirect light to partial shade; N'Joy holds its crisp variegation better in bright light than deep shade.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in bright, indirect light to partial shade, out of direct hot sun that can scorch the white leaf portions. N'Joy is a compact pothos sport with smaller leaves than standard golden or Marble Queen pothos, each crisply divided into bold, clean patches of white and green rather than the finer marbling of other variegated types, giving it a tidy, high-contrast look well suited to small pots, shelves, and desks. It trails or climbs on a support and stays more compact and slower-growing than larger-leaved pothos cultivars, which keeps it tidy for a longer stretch between prunings. Let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings, since pothos is prone to root rot in constantly soggy soil, and in zone 9a it can spend summer outdoors in shade but must come inside before frost.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained potting mix in bright indirect light to partial shade; Jessenia grows faster and tolerates lower light better than heavily white-variegated pothos cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in bright, indirect light to partial shade. Jessenia is a pothos sport with heart-shaped leaves marbled in light chartreuse-gold and mid-green, a softer, more evenly blended variegation pattern than the sharp white patches of Marble Queen or N'Joy, giving it a warmer overall color that reads almost golden from a distance. Because it carries less pure-white tissue than heavily variegated cultivars, it grows more vigorously and tolerates lower indoor light without reverting to solid green as readily. It trails or climbs on a support and is a forgiving, low-maintenance houseplant; let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings and bring outdoor summer containers inside well before frost in zone 9a.

common_name: Global Green Pothos (Subtle Green-on-Green Marbled Pothos)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained potting mix in bright indirect light to partial shade; Global Green tolerates lower light better than white-variegated pothos since it carries no pure-white tissue.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in bright, indirect light to partial shade. Global Green is a newer pothos cultivar with a subtle, two-toned marbling of dark and lime green across each leaf rather than the white or gold variegation of most popular pothos, giving it a quieter, more textural look that reads as solid green from a distance but reveals rich patterning up close. Because the variegation is entirely green-based rather than white, the plant photosynthesizes more efficiently than heavily white-marked cultivars and tolerates lower indoor light with less risk of reverting or stalling. It trails or climbs readily on a support; let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings and bring outdoor summer containers indoors before frost in zone 9a.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained potting mix in low to bright indirect light; Jade pothos is the most shade- and low-light-tolerant pothos cultivar since it carries no variegation to maintain.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in low to bright indirect light; unlike its variegated relatives, Jade pothos has solid, uniformly deep green, glossy heart-shaped leaves with no white or gold patterning to fade or scorch, making it the toughest and most shade-tolerant pothos for dim interior corners, offices, and bathrooms with little natural light. It grows quickly and vigorously in these low-light settings, where variegated cultivars would slow or revert to green anyway, and trails or climbs readily on a support or moss pole. Let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings, since pothos is prone to root rot in constantly wet soil, and in zone 9a it can summer outdoors in shade but must come inside well before frost.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Moonlight philodendron is frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere as an indoor plant.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix. Moonlight is a compact, non-climbing, self-heading philodendron whose new leaves emerge a striking bright chartreuse-yellow before slowly deepening to a richer lime-green as they age, so an actively growing plant always carries a glowing cluster of fresh yellow-green foliage at its center. Its neat rosette habit and modest size need no staking or climbing support, making it a tidy tabletop or shelf specimen as much as a floor plant. Give it bright, indirect light for the best color, since low light dulls the chartreuse tone toward plain green, but avoid direct sun, which can scorch the tender young leaves. Let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container plant; Rosso Peperomia cannot survive frost. In zone 9, grow in a container that can be moved indoors when temperatures drop below 50°F, and use a small pot, since Peperomia prefers to be slightly root-bound.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade, avoiding direct sun, which bleaches and scorches the leaves. Rosso is a compact, rosette-forming Peperomia caperata cultivar with deeply corrugated, dark olive-green, arrow-shaped leaves that carry a striking deep red-burgundy underside and matching red petioles, so a bird's-eye view shows dark green ruffled tops while a glance from below or the side reveals the vivid red reverse. The plant stays small and tidy indefinitely, making it well suited to small pots, terrariums, and desktop or shelf display alongside other compact houseplants. Watering is the main cultural challenge, since the succulent stems and leaves store considerable water and rot quickly if kept too wet; allow the top inch or two of soil to dry completely between waterings.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Peperomia species for indoor use

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging container; Hope Peperomia cannot survive frost. In zone 9, grow in a container that can be moved indoors when temperatures drop below 50°F, using a small pot since Peperomia prefers to be slightly root-bound.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade in a hanging basket or elevated pot where the trailing stems can cascade, avoiding direct sun, which scorches the leaves. Hope is a naturally occurring Peperomia hybrid with small, round, thick, succulent, glossy green leaves densely packed along slender trailing stems, giving a fuller, more cascading habit than the rosette-forming Peperomia species grown mainly for patterned single leaves. Its compact, easy-care nature and trailing form make it a popular choice for hanging baskets, shelves, and terrariums where the stems can spill over an edge. Like other Peperomias it stores water in its succulent leaves and stems and is prone to root rot if overwatered, so allow the top inch or two of soil to dry completely between waterings, and pinch stem tips to encourage fuller, bushier growth.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container with a moss pole or trellis for support; Peru Monstera is frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere as an indoor plant.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich, aroid-style potting mix, providing a moss pole or trellis for the climbing stems to grip as the plant matures. Peru Monstera, sold under the species name Monstera karstenianum, produces small, thick, deeply quilted or puckered, dark green leaves with a pronounced glossy, almost armored texture unlike the smooth, thin leaves and large fenestrations of the better-known Monstera deliciosa. Its more compact leaf size and modest overall footprint make it manageable as a climbing houseplant even in smaller rooms, while still showing off distinctive rippled foliage texture as a talking point. Let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings and mist occasionally or use a pebble tray to support the higher humidity this species prefers indoors.
